qs.q: A 67-year-old man dies six months after suffering a large putaminal hemorrhage. Coronal brain slices through the basal ganglia at autopsy demonstrate which appearance at the site of the old lesion?
o: Firm glial scar without cystic space
qs.e: An old, remote hemorrhage evolves into a cavitary lesion with a golden-brown wall due to hemosiderin-laden macrophages. Fresh coagula and liquefactive necrosis characterize acute and subacute stages rather than fully healed remote cavities.

qs.q: Which of the following structures is NOT considered part of the basal ganglia?
qs.e: The dentate nucleus is part of the cerebellum, not the basal ganglia, serving as a deep cerebellar nucleus for motor coordination. The basal ganglia properly include the caudate nucleus, putamen, and globus pallidus.

qs.q: Which specific anatomical structures combine to form the striatum within the basal ganglia circuitry?
qs.e: The caudate nucleus and the putamen collectively form the striatum, whereas the putamen and globus pallidus form the lentiform nucleus. The globus pallidus sits internally to these structures.

qs.q: What is the primary neurochemical nature of the afferent signal projecting from the cerebral cortex to the striatum within the basal ganglia pathways?
qs.e: Afferents from the cerebral cortex to the striatum are excitatory and use glutamate as their neurotransmitter. Substantia nigra pars compacta inputs to the striatum provide dopaminergic modulation instead.

qs.q: During a clinical review of basal ganglia motor circuits, a resident is asked which structures serve as the main output nuclei projecting directly to the thalamus. Which pair represents these output structures?
o: Globus pallidus interna and substantia nigra pars reticulata
External globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus
Substantia nigra pars compacta and striatum
qs.e: The globus pallidus interna and the substantia nigra pars reticulata serve as the primary efferent output nuclei projecting to the thalamus. The striatum serves as the major input receptor region receiving cortical signals.

qs.q: A 44-year-old woman dies of a basal ganglia hemorrhage. She has LVH (550g heart), small scarred kidneys, and arterioles with concentric intimal thickening. Most likely condition?
qs.e: LVH + CNS hemorrhage + small kidneys + hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis = malignant hypertension with multi-organ end-organ damage.

qs.q: Which component of the basal ganglia plays the major role in the control of cognitive (memory-guided) motor activity?
qs.e: The caudate nucleus is part of the associative circuit of the basal ganglia and plays a major role in cognitive aspects of motor control, including memory-guided movements and executive motor functions. The putamen is more involved in automatic motor patterns, while the other structures have different roles in basal ganglia function.

qs.q: Basal ganglia neurotransmitters include all except ---
qs.e: Glycine is primarily found in the spinal cord and brainstem, not as a major basal ganglia neurotransmitter.

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The basal ganglia are deep brain nuclei that modulate movement and cognition. Their dysfunction leads to movement disorders and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Clinicians must link clinical signs to specific nuclei and pathways.

sections.p: The basal ganglia are a group of subcortical nuclei that regulate motor output, habit formation, and reward. They form closed loops with cortex and thalamus, balancing excitation and inhibition.
b: Key nuclei: caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra

sections.p: They lie in the lateral and medial basal forebrain, surrounded by the internal capsule and adjacent to the lateral ventricles. Each nucleus has distinct cytoarchitecture.
b: Caudate head sits beside lateral ventricle
Putamen forms lateral part of lentiform nucleus

sections.p: The basal ganglia are intimately related to the internal capsule, thalamus, and cortex. Their deep location makes them vulnerable to hemorrhage and ischemia.
They receive arterial blood from branches of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) and anterior choroidal artery. The lenticulostriate arteries are critical feeders.
b: Lenticulostriate arteries supply caudate and putamen

t.b: Shows vessel stenosis or aneurysm causing hemorrhage; abnormal flow indicates risk of stroke
Detects acute ischemia in basal ganglia; helps differentiate hemorrhage from infarct

sections.p: The basal ganglia receive cortical inputs via the cortico-striatal pathway and send outputs through the thalamus to cortex. They are modulated by dopaminergic neurons from the substantia nigra.
They regulate movement by balancing the direct (facilitatory) and indirect (inhibitory) pathways. They also influence reward, habit, and executive functions.
b: Direct pathway: disinhibits thalamus to promote movement

sections.p: Hemorrhage, ischemia, and neurodegeneration (Parkinson’s, Huntington’s) affect basal ganglia. Symptoms vary from rigidity to chorea to cognitive decline.
b: Hemorrhage presents with sudden focal deficits and increased intracranial pressure

t.b: Detects hyperdense hemorrhage; guides emergency surgery
Shows chronic lesions in Huntington’s; identifies demyelination in infections

sections.p: Remember the direct vs indirect pathway balance. In Parkinson’s, loss of dopaminergic neurons shifts the balance toward the indirect pathway, causing rigidity.
b: Direct pathway: striatum → GPi → thalamus → cortex

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache with focal neurological signs (possible basal ganglia hemorrhage)
Rapid onset of rigidity or tremor with bradykinesia (possible Parkinsonian crisis)

faq.q: What causes basal ganglia hemorrhage in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Hypertension, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and malaria‑associated vasculitis are common culprits.

faq.q: How does Parkinson’s disease affect the basal ganglia?
faq.a: Loss of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra increases indirect pathway activity, leading to over‑inhibition of thalamocortical drive.

faq.q: Can infections damage the basal ganglia?
faq.a: Yes; tuberculosis, HIV, and neurocysticercosis can cause focal lesions or diffuse inflammation.
